notes.bp: Packet loss removes evidence rather than merely adding noise; a universal enhancer must reconstruct missing regions and then handle other distortions.
notes.wh: Lost segments interact with noise, reverberation, clipping, bandwidth limits, codec damage, and residual loss.
notes.naive: Use one denoiser and assume missing samples behave like ordinary noise.
notes.ap: Use a three-stage pipeline: filling, separation, and restoration.
notes.mech: The filling stage predicts lost regions, separation suppresses noise/reverb/clipping, and restoration repairs bandwidth, codec, and remaining loss.
notes.math: Stage-wise spectral or waveform reconstruction is evaluated in the URGENT challenge setting.
notes.dots: Packet loss is a missing-evidence problem and should not be collapsed into generic denoising.
notes.ww: The system ranked second in URGENT Track 1.
notes.limits: Challenge conditions, author-reported ranking, and no independent run limit the claim.

notes.bp: Open-vocabulary keyword spotting must find arbitrary words without preparing word-aligned training data for every target.
notes.wh: Forced alignment is costly, while streaming recognition cannot wait for a separately aligned corpus.
notes.naive: Build a fixed-vocabulary detector or use an external forced aligner and precomputed word segments.
notes.ap: Integrate W-CTC forced alignment into a fully end-to-end streaming system.
notes.mech: CTC paths supply word-span alignment while the text encoder and verifier are trained in the same pipeline.
notes.math: CTC alignment links acoustic frames to text; keyword audio-text similarity then scores arbitrary words.
notes.dots: Open vocabulary is a training and alignment problem, not only a larger keyword list.
notes.ww: The paper reports superior performance on the Libriphrase hard set.
notes.limits: Benchmark, language, and author-reported result limit generalization and independent reproducibility.

notes.bp: Silent-speech decoding could let speech-impaired users communicate without vocalizing, but biosignal recordings vary across people and electrode layouts.
notes.wh: EEG and EMG configurations are heterogeneous and patient data are scarce, so a single fixed-subject model does not transfer well.
notes.naive: Train one model per subject with one fixed electrode configuration.
notes.ap: Handle heterogeneous electrodes and use multitask training for cross-subject and cross-language calibration.
notes.mech: A shared model learns from varying EEG/EMG layouts while multitask objectives stabilize word classification across speakers and languages.
notes.math: Word classification accuracy measures whether neural signals preserve enough information for decoding.
notes.dots: Assistive speech is constrained by sensing hardware and patient variation as much as by the decoder.
notes.ww: Accuracy is 95.3% for healthy participants and 54.5% for a patient, versus 70.1% and 13.2% for single-subject baselines.
notes.limits: Patient count, setup, calibration, and author-reported results limit clinical deployment claims.
